533.title: Your faith has made you well (Luke 8:40–56)
533.hook: a bleeding woman and a dying girl, twelve years each
533.howItsDone: Some Christians pray with the healing of the woman and Jairus's daughter when they or someone they love is ill, and in some churches prayer for the sick includes a gentle touch on the shoulder or hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a storm on the lake and a man among the tombs, sent home. Your line was return to your house. Whose storm did you help calm? Day five hundred thirty-three.

Twelve years. That's the number tying today's two stories together. A man named Jairus, a ruler of the local synagogue, an important man in town, falls at Jesus' feet. His only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying. Please come. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses so tightly around him that it's hard to move. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody notices, who has been bleeding for twelve years. As long as Jairus's daughter has been alive, this woman has been sick. Luke says she had spent everything she had on doctors, and none of them could heal her. She doesn't ask for anything. She has a plan.

Under the law of her time, her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and for twelve years that would have kept her at the edges of worship and of ordinary touch. So she comes up from behind and, in the King James words, "touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched." She just wanted to slip away. But Jesus stops. "Who touched me?" Peter points out the obvious: Master, the whole crowd is pressing against you! But Jesus says, "Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me." Virtue here means power. Trembling, she comes forward and tells everything in front of everyone. And Jesus says: "Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace." Daughter. A family word for a woman who had been kept at the edges, said in public, so the whole town hears that she is well. Made thee whole is the Greek sozo. It's the same phrase as "thy faith hath saved thee," said to the woman at Simon's dinner. Healed and saved share one word. But the stop has cost time. A messenger arrives: "Thy daughter is dead; trouble not the Master." Jesus hears it and says: "Fear not: believe only, and she shall be made whole." At the house, the mourners are already wailing. He says she's sleeping, and they laugh at him. He takes her hand: "Maid, arise." She gets up. And then a very practical line: he tells them to give her something to eat.
screen: `SHE TOUCHED THE BORDER OF HIS GARMENT.`
`DAUGHTER: THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`
then, large: `FEAR NOT: BELIEVE ONLY, AND SHE SHALL BE MADE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two people at once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two people who need help right now. One might be loud about it, like Jairus, important and urgent and asking. The other might be quiet, like the woman in the crowd, hidden, hoping nobody notices. Hold them both. Notice which one your attention runs to first. Then bring the other one forward, too. In the story, Jesus has time for both: he stops for the woman and still reaches the girl. Breathe in for one person, breathe out for the other, back and forth. If you pray, you can hold both before God together. If you don't, simply keep both in your care. The bell holds the time.
Sozo, the Greek word used for both healing and being saved: Jesus' words to a woman healed after twelve years, said on the way to a twelve-year-old girl he raises with a word, maid, arise.
Your line: only believe. Today, hold your two people together, and do one small thing for the quiet one. Day five hundred thirty-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: a healing story with a happy ending.
what it means: Jesus stops for the hidden woman and makes her healing public, then raises a girl everyone else had given up on.
what a scholar hears: "thy faith hath made thee whole" here and "thy faith hath saved thee" at Simon's dinner (7:50) are the same Greek words, built on sozo.

534.title: The twelve sent out (Luke 9:1–17)
534.hook: sent with nothing, then the five thousand fed
534.carry: you give them something to eat
534.howItsDone: Some Christian food pantries and church meal programs take "give ye them to eat" as a motto, and Christians often notice in this meal the actions of the Last Supper and communion: taking, blessing, breaking and giving bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman in the crowd and a girl who got up and ate. Your line was only believe. Did you do one small thing for the quiet one of your two? Day five hundred thirty-four.

No walking stick, no bag, no bread, no money, no spare clothes. That's the packing list Jesus gives the twelve. In the King James words: "Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece." A scrip is a traveler's bag. So they go out empty-handed, village by village, to preach and to heal, depending on whoever opens a door. Until now they've watched. Now they're sent. And it works. Word spreads so far that Herod himself, who had John beheaded, hears about it and is perplexed. Who is this? He wants to see him.
screen: `NO STAFF, NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.`

segments.voice: The twelve come back full of stories, and Jesus takes them aside privately, to a deserted place near a town called Bethsaida. But the crowds follow. Luke says Jesus "received them," welcomed them, spoke about the kingdom, healed those who needed it. Hours pass. The sun gets low. And the twelve, sensibly, come to him: "Send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals: for we are here in a desert place." It's a reasonable plan. It's what any good organizer would say. And Jesus answers, short and plain: "Give ye them to eat." You. You feed them. They've just come back from a journey where they carried nothing. Now he hands the problem back to them. They count what they have: "We have no more but five loaves and two fishes." About five thousand men, Luke says. Jesus has them sit down in groups of about fifty, like guests at a meal. Then he takes the five loaves and two fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives to the disciples to set before the crowd. Later in Luke, at the Last Supper, nearly the same movements return: took, gave thanks, broke, gave. Everyone eats. Everyone is filled. And they pick up the leftovers: twelve baskets. Some readers notice: one for each of the twelve who said send them away. Jesus didn't do it without them. He did it through their hands, with what they already had, which was almost nothing.
screen: then, large: `GIVE YE THEM TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go without one comfort today. Settle, and breathe. The twelve went out with nothing extra and found they had enough. Think of one small comfort you could set aside for a day: the second coffee, the snack, the streaming show, the online shopping, the extra blanket of scrolling before sleep. Not as punishment. As a way of noticing how much you usually carry. Picture the day without it. Then think: what could that small saving, of money or time, become in someone else's hands? A meal, a gift, an hour for someone. Five loaves and two fish. If you pray, you can offer that small thing to God. If you don't, simply decide where it goes. The bell holds the time.
Scrip, an old word for a traveler's bag: Jesus sends the twelve out with nothing, then hands them a hungry crowd and five loaves, and through their hands five thousand are fed.
Your line: you give them something to eat. Skip your one comfort today, and let what it saves feed someone. Day five hundred thirty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus fed five thousand people by himself.
what it means: he hands the problem to the disciples, takes their almost-nothing, and feeds everyone through their hands.
what a scholar hears: took, blessed, broke and gave are nearly the actions Luke repeats at the Last Supper, where Jesus gives thanks, so readers hear that meal ahead in this one.

535.title: Daily cross (Luke 9:18–27)
535.hook: Luke adds one word: take up your cross daily
535.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of "carrying their cross" for the ordinary burdens of daily life, and in many traditions the daily offering of one's day to God is a morning practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve sent out, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was you give them something to eat. What did your skipped comfort become for someone else? Day five hundred thirty-five.

Matthew, Mark and Luke all record the same hard saying: if anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself and take up his cross. But Luke's version has one extra word. Just one. It is easy to miss, and once you see it, the whole sentence changes shape. It comes right after a quiet moment. Luke says Jesus was "alone praying," with only his disciples nearby. Again, prayer at a turning point. And when he finishes, he asks them a question, the kind you'd ask your closest friends late at night when the crowd has gone home: "Whom say the people that I am?"
screen: `WHOM SAY THE PEOPLE THAT I AM?`

segments.voice: They report the gossip: some say John the Baptist, back from the dead; others Elijah; others one of the old prophets. Then he makes it personal: "But whom say ye that I am?" And Peter answers: "The Christ of God." Christ means anointed one, the Messiah, the king Israel hoped for. And immediately Jesus tells them not to spread it, and says something nobody expected a Messiah to say: "The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day." Then, to everyone: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." There it is. Daily. In Greek, kath hemeran, day by day. Matthew and Mark don't have it. In Rome's world, a cross wasn't a symbol. It was how the empire executed rebels and slaves, and the condemned man carried the crossbeam himself through the streets. Taking up your cross meant walking toward the end. Matthew and Mark say it like a single great decision. Luke adds daily, and the picture shifts: not one dramatic moment, but a thing you pick up again every morning. Christians across the centuries have heard it both ways at once. Some have literally faced death for their faith. Most have faced the ordinary kind: putting someone else first again today, keeping a promise again today, not getting their own way again today. "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it." In Luke, losing your life happens one day at a time.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE? THE CHRIST OF GOD.`
then, large: `TAKE UP HIS CROSS DAILY, AND FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one daily faithful thing. Settle, and breathe. Think about the ordinary weight you carry every day, the thing that's yours to pick up whether you feel like it or not. Caring for a parent. Showing up to a job that's hard. Being patient with a child, or with your own body. Staying honest when no one would know. Don't make it bigger than it is, and don't make it smaller. Just see it. Then picture tomorrow morning, picking it up again, on purpose this time, not grudgingly. Imagine doing it with a little love in it. If you pray, you can offer that daily weight to God. If you don't, simply choose to carry it with care. The bell holds the time.
Daily cross. Peter names Jesus the Christ of God, and Jesus says anyone who follows him must take up the cross, and Luke adds the word daily.
Your line: daily. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, pick up your ordinary weight on purpose. And today, carry it one more time with care. Day five hundred thirty-five.

what it means: Luke adds daily, so the cross becomes something picked up again every morning, in ordinary faithfulness.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 16:24 and Mark 8:34 lack kath hemeran; Luke's addition turns a once-for-all call into a daily rhythm.

536.title: His face shone (Luke 9:28–36)
536.hook: he was praying when his face changed; Moses and Elijah talk of his departure
536.howItsDone: Churches in several traditions keep a feast of the Transfiguration, and some Protestant churches mark Transfiguration Sunday just before Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's answer and the daily cross. Your line was daily. Did you pick up your ordinary weight on purpose this morning? Day five hundred thirty-six.

About eight days after the talk of the cross, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, John and James, and climbs a mountain. Luke tells us why: they went up "to pray." Some people describe a place, a hospital chapel, a hilltop, a kitchen at 4am, where they sat in prayer or silence long enough that something in the room seemed to change. Not dramatically. Just a shift. The three disciples are tired. Luke says they were "heavy with sleep." And while they're fighting to keep their eyes open, Jesus keeps praying. And then his face begins to change.

In the King James words: "And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering." As he prayed. That's Luke's own emphasis. Matthew says his face did shine as the sun; Luke says it changed while he was praying. The light comes in the middle of prayer. Then two men are talking with him, Moses and Elijah, the lawgiver and the prophet. In Exodus, Moses' own face shone after he spoke with God on a mountain. And what are they talking about? Luke tells us: they "spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem." Decease, in Greek, is exodos: a departure, a way out. Some readers hear in it the book of Exodus, the story of Moses leading Israel out of slavery. Here, standing next to Moses, Jesus talks about his own exodus, the death and rising waiting for him in Jerusalem. Peter wakes up enough to say something, anything: "Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles." Three shelters, three tents. Stay, make it last. Luke adds kindly that he didn't know what he was saying. Then a cloud covers them, and a voice: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." When the cloud lifts, Jesus is alone. And they tell no one in those days. Churches remember this as the Transfiguration, the change of form. But in Luke, the change doesn't come from nowhere. It comes while he prays.
screen: then, large: `AS HE PRAYED, THE FASHION OF HIS COUNTENANCE WAS ALTERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay in the quiet until something shifts. Settle, and breathe. Don't aim for a vision. Aim for staying. Close your eyes and let yourself sit past the point where you'd normally stop. The first minute is often noisy: lists, worries, tiredness, like the disciples heavy with sleep. Keep going. Breathe. Notice the moment, if it comes, when something softens. A thought loosens. Your shoulders drop. The noise thins. It might be very small. Don't grab at it, the way Peter wanted to build shelters. Just notice it. If you pray, you can let the words run out and simply stay. If you don't, simply stay. The bell holds the time.

Exodos, Greek for a going out, a departure: on a mountain, while Jesus prays, his face changes and his clothes blaze white, and Moses and Elijah speak with him about his coming death and rising at Jerusalem.
Your line: while he prayed. Today, find one quiet stretch and stay in it a little longer than feels natural. Notice what shifts. Day five hundred thirty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus glowed on a mountain.
what it means: in Luke, the change comes while he prays, and Moses and Elijah talk with him about what waits in Jerusalem.

537.title: Whoever is least (Luke 9:37–50)
537.hook: a boy healed, an argument about greatness, a child set beside him
537.howItsDone: Some churches point to Luke 9:48 in their work with children, from Sunday schools to child-protection and welcome policies, as a sign that receiving a child is receiving Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mountain, a changed face, and Moses and Elijah talking about an exodus. Your line was while he prayed. Did you stay in the quiet a little longer? Day five hundred thirty-seven.

The next day they come down the mountain, and a crowd is waiting, and a father is shouting over the noise. "Master, I beseech thee, look upon my son: for he is mine only child." Luke says a spirit seizes the boy, throws him into convulsions and leaves him bruised. And the father adds the painful part: "I besought thy disciples to cast him out; and they could not." The disciples who stayed below have failed in front of everyone. Jesus' answer is weary, almost a sigh at the whole generation: how long shall I be with you? Then, simply: "Bring thy son hither."
screen: `LOOK UPON MY SON: MINE ONLY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Even as the boy is brought, he's thrown down again. Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the child, and, in the King James words, "delivered him again to his father." Gave him back. The same gesture as the widow's son at Nain. The crowd is "amazed at the mighty power of God." And while everyone is marveling, Jesus tells his disciples something hard: the Son of man will be delivered into human hands. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask. Then, Luke says, a strange thing: "there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest." Right after failing to heal a boy. Right after hearing their teacher will be handed over. They argue about rank. Jesus knows what they're thinking, and he answers without a speech. He "took a child, and set him by him." Next to himself. The disciples have been arguing about rank, and a child has none to offer. And he says: "Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great." Welcome this child, and you welcome Jesus, and the one who sent him. Then John, a little too quickly, reports: we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we stopped him, because he isn't one of us. Jesus: "Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us." Two lessons in a row against the same instinct: to rank people, and to guard the circle.
screen: then, large: `HE THAT IS LEAST AMONG YOU ALL, THE SAME SHALL BE GREAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put a child's need first. Settle, and breathe. Picture Jesus taking a child by the hand and setting them next to him, while the grown-ups go quiet. Now think of a child in your life: your own, a niece or nephew, a neighbor's kid, a student, a child you sponsor, or the child you once were. What do they need right now that's easy to overlook because adult things feel more urgent? Time. Attention. A meal, a ride, a bedtime story, a promise kept. Let one need come clearly. Then picture putting it first today, ahead of something that seemed more important. If you pray, you can hold that child before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Whoever is least. While the disciples argue about who is greatest, Jesus sets a child beside him and says the least among you is the one who is great.
Your line: the least is the greatest. Today, put one child's need ahead of something that felt more important, and notice who gets the seat beside you. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

what a scholar hears: Luke calls three people in his healing stories an "only" child, monogenes: the widow's son, Jairus's daughter and this boy.

538.title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
538.hook: he turns toward Jerusalem; foxes have holes, but he has nowhere to lay his head
538.howItsDone: Commentators call this long stretch of Luke the travel narrative, and some Christians read through it slowly, a few verses a day, as a journey toward Jerusalem and Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child set beside Jesus while the disciples argued about rank. Your line was the least is the greatest. Whose need did you put first? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Here, halfway through chapter nine, Luke's Gospel turns a corner, and you can almost feel the road tilt. In the King James words: "when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." From here on, Jesus is walking. The Good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus in the tree: Luke sets them on the road to Jerusalem, the city where Jesus has already said what is waiting. Set his face. Some readers hear an echo of the prophet Isaiah, where God's servant says: "therefore have I set my face like a flint." Flint. Hard stone. Not stubbornness. Resolve.

The road goes through Samaria first. In John's Gospel, a Samaritan woman names one old dispute between Samaritans and Jews: where the right place to worship is. Jesus sends messengers ahead to find a place to stay, and a Samaritan village turns them away, Luke says, because he was heading to Jerusalem. James and John are furious: "Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" Fire from heaven, like Elijah. And Luke says: "he turned, and rebuked them." They simply go to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you anywhere. Jesus answers: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Anywhere includes nowhere. To the second, Jesus says: follow me. The man says, let me first go and bury my father. And Jesus says something startling: "Let the dead bury their dead." Readers differ on what it meant: some think the father had just died, others that the man meant to wait until his father died someday. The text doesn't say. What's clear is the urgency. The third says, let me first say goodbye to my family. And Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." It's a plowman's picture: look back over your shoulder and the furrow goes crooked. You keep your eyes on a point ahead, and you walk toward it.
screen: `HAND TO THE PLOUGH, NO LOOKING BACK.`
then, large: `HE STEDFASTLY SET HIS FACE TO GO TO JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set your face toward one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you keep circling and not doing. A hard conversation. A doctor's appointment. A debt to face, an apology to make, a job application, a habit to end. Let one come up. Notice how you usually look back: the excuses, the let-me-first, the someday. Now picture a plowman with a point fixed on the far side of the field. Picture your face set toward your hard thing, calm, steady, flint, not angry. Choose the very first step, the one you could take today. If you pray, you can ask for a steady face. If you don't, simply fix your eyes on the step. The bell holds the time.
Flint, the hard stone Isaiah uses for an unbending resolve: Luke's turning point, where Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem and will not be turned back.
Your line: no looking back. Take the first step toward your hard thing today, and when the let-me-first voices start, keep your eyes on the point ahead. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: Seventy sent (Luke 10:1–20)
539.hook: sent in pairs: say peace to this house first
539.howItsDone: In the Book of Common Prayer, the order for the visitation of the sick opens with "Peace be to this house," and some Christians use the same words when blessing a home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he set his face toward Jerusalem. Your line was no looking back. Did you take the first step toward your hard thing? Day five hundred thirty-nine.

What's the first thing you say when you walk into someone's home? Hi. Sorry I'm late. Where should I put my shoes? Something smells amazing. Jesus is now on the road to Jerusalem, and he sends out a much bigger group than the twelve. In the King James words: "the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come." Two by two. No one goes alone. Ahead of him, like people preparing the way. And before anything else, he tells them exactly what to say when they walk through a door.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: First, the honest warning: "The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few." And: "behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves." Not soldiers. Lambs. Then the packing list again, lighter than ever: no purse, no bag, no shoes, and don't stop to chat with everyone on the road. Then the doorway. "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." First. Before the message, before the meal, before anything. Behind the Greek word for peace stands the Hebrew greeting shalom, which reaches past the absence of fighting toward wholeness and well-being. Then a beautiful detail: "And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again." Peace is like something you set down in a room. If someone there is open to it, it stays. If not, it comes back to you. You don't lose it by offering it. Stay in one house, he says. Eat what they put in front of you. Heal the sick. Say the kingdom of God has come near. And if a town won't welcome you, shake off the dust and move on. The seventy come back overjoyed: even the demons obey us in your name! And Jesus, gently, turns their joy in a better direction: "rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." Not in the power they had, he says, but in being known by name. Luke never names them. They aren't the twelve. They're a crowd of followers, sent ahead to the places he himself would come.
screen: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`
then, large: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say peace to a house. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a home you'll walk into soon. Your own, after work. A friend's. A parent's. A home where things are tense right now, or simply tired. Picture yourself at the door. Before you say anything about the traffic or what's for dinner, picture yourself bringing peace in with you, quietly, like setting down a gift. You don't have to say the words aloud. You can carry them in. Then let go of whether it's received. If it rests there, good. If not, it comes back to you. If you pray, you can say the line from Luke silently at the door. If you don't, simply bring calm in with you. The bell holds the time.
Seventy sent. Jesus sends out seventy, two by two, as lambs among wolves, and tells them to say first, at every door: peace be to this house.

Your line: peace be to this house. Bring it through the next door you open. And look back at the week: a hidden woman and a waking girl, five loaves, a daily cross, a shining face, a child, a road, and seventy at the door. Day five hundred thirty-nine, and another week on the path.

fork.setup: you're one of the seventy, at the door of a stranger's house. what do you say first?
fork.reveal: peace comes first. if a son of peace is there, it rests on the house; if not, it returns to you.

original.note: Greek: peace. in Jesus' world the greeting was shalom: wholeness and well-being.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mission trip.
what it means: seventy ordinary followers sent ahead in pairs, told to offer peace first at every door and let it rest or return.
what a scholar hears: "before his face" is the phrase Luke used a chapter earlier for the messengers sent ahead into Samaria (9:52): the seventy go to prepare his road.
